name: Canon AE-1 Program
summary: The camera that put full program auto-exposure into Canon's mainstream SLR line.
description: Program mode is the point of it. The camera sets both shutter speed and aperture on its own, and steps back to shutter priority or full manual when it is told to.
It is an electronic body, so without a battery it will not fire at all.
That combination, a program mode that asks nothing of the person holding it and a body sold in enormous numbers, is why it is so often somebody's first SLR.

name: Canon Autoboy FXL
summary: Canon's pocket compact with a fixed wide-angle prime, an upgrade of the Sure Shot M.
description: It replaced the Sure Shot M and kept the same idea: one focal length, no zoom, and a body small enough to carry without having decided to.
Canon sold it under three names by region, which is most of why it is hard to look up. Sure Shot Sleek in the Americas, Prima Mini II in Europe, Autoboy F XL in Japan.

name: Canon Autoboy S
summary: A zoom compact with a 38 to 115mm lens, sold as the Sure Shot Z115 in the Americas and the Prima Super 115 in Europe.
description: The lens is ten elements in nine groups, one of them aspherical, and opens to f/3.6 at the wide end. It focuses to 0.6m, and to 0.4m in macro.

Focus is three-point autofocus on a near-infrared beam and can be prefocused. Exposure is fully automatic: a programmed shutter running from 2 seconds to 1/1200 depending on mode and focal length, metered across three zones over EV 2 to 21. There is no aperture or shutter control, and a dial on the back picks a scene mode instead.

At 350g on two CR123A cells it is a lot of camera to carry for a compact. The cost of the 3x range is the long end, where the maximum aperture falls to f/8.5 and you are on flash or fast film well before 115mm.

name: Fujica ST605 II
summary: The last Fujica SLR to use the M42 screw mount, sold only in Asia in the late 1970s.
description: It arrived while Fuji was moving to its own X bayonet, so it was sold briefly and in one region, which is why it is uncommon anywhere else.
Being M42, it takes the enormous supply of screw-mount lenses that every maker built for, and that is most of the argument for owning one now.

name: Fujifilm QuickSnap Flash 400
summary: A single-use camera Fujifilm pre-loads with a 27-exposure roll of ISO 400 color film.
description: One fixed-focus plastic lens, one shutter speed, and a viewfinder that only approximates what the lens sees. Fujifilm loads it with 27 exposures of Fujicolor Superia X-TRA 400.

The flash is the part worth knowing. It reaches about ten feet, recharges by itself, can be left switched on, and has a manual switch, which is more control than the rest of the camera offers put together.
Everything else is fixed, so it works in bright sun and under the flash, and not much in between.

name: Hasselblad XPan
summary: A rangefinder Hasselblad and Fujifilm launched in 1998 that switches between 24x36mm and 24x65mm frames on one roll.
description: Fujifilm designed and built it, in Japan, and sold the same camera as the TX-1.

The panoramic frame is the native one. The gate is 24x65mm and the three Fujinon lenses, a 45mm f/4, a 90mm f/4 and a 30mm f/5.6, were computed to cover it; selecting the standard frame masks down from that rather than the other way round. The 30mm needs its own finder and a center filter.

The rangefinder moves its frame lines and parallax correction for the mounted lens and the chosen format. The body is titanium, exposure is aperture priority or manual behind a vertical metal shutter running 8 seconds to 1/1000, and none of it works without two CR2 cells. A 36-exposure roll gives 21 panoramic frames.

name: Kodak Cameo Auto Focus QD
summary: A compact autofocus point-and-shoot from Kodak's 1990s Cameo series, with a quartz date back.
description: The lens is an Ektanar with two-zone autofocus, focusing from about 0.8m to infinity. Film advance and rewind are motorized, and film speed is read off the DX code across ISO 100 to 400.
The flash fires automatically in low light, with a guide number of 8m at ISO 100.
It is small and light, roughly 123 by 69 by 33mm and 170g on a lithium cell, and it adds a switchable panoramic mask and a self-timer. QD is the quartz date imprint.

name: Kodak FunSaver
summary: A single-use camera Kodak pre-loads with a 27-exposure roll of its 800-speed color film.
description: A 40mm lens, a built-in flash, and 27 exposures of Kodak Gold 800 already inside. The developed strip is edge-marked GT 800.
Kodak sells the loaded film on sharpness, fine grain for its speed, and color that holds up across mixed lighting.
The body is meant to be handed in whole and recycled when the lab opens it, which is the part of the design that is not about photography.

name: Kodak Snapic A1
summary: A modern reusable full-frame compact with a three-element glass lens, made by RETO under Kodak license.
description: RETO makes and sells it under license. The glass lens is what separates it from the plastic-lensed reusables it sits beside on the shelf, including RETO's own half-frame cameras.
It has two-zone focus and a double-exposure switch, which is unusual at the price and is most of the reason to pick it up.

name: Konica K-mini
summary: A pocket fixed-focus compact Konica built around a 28mm lens and a sliding cover.
description: The lens is a Konica 28mm f/6.7, three elements in three groups, fixed focus from about 0.9m to infinity. There is nothing to set. An electronically programmed shutter with three speeds between 1/60 and 1/180 doubles as the aperture, and film speed comes off the DX code across ISO 100 to 400.
Sliding the lens cover open powers it up. Loading, advance and rewind are motorized, and the flash fires by itself in low light on a five second recycle.
The viewfinder is a Galilean inverted type at 0.45x, which is small and dim. At 135g without the battery, that is the trade it makes.

name: Lomography Sprocket Rocket
summary: A panoramic camera that exposes across the sprocket holes for a 1:3 wide image.
description: The frame is 34 by 72mm, which runs off the edge of the picture area and over the perforations, so the sprocket holes print as part of the image. A mask is supplied to crop back to 24 by 72mm for anyone who does not want them.
Winding is manual in both directions, and the reverse gear is there so frames can be wound back and overlapped on purpose.
It is a plastic camera with one job, and it does not do the ordinary one. There is no way to get a normal 35mm frame out of it.

name: Olympus 35 SP
summary: A fixed-lens rangefinder Olympus made from 1969, with both center-weighted and spot metering.
description: The lens is a G.Zuiko 42mm f/1.7, seven elements in five groups on a double-Gauss design, taking 49mm filters, with a Copal leaf shutter behind it running 1 second to 1/500 and Bulb.
The metering is the reason to want one. A CdS cell reads either a center-weighted average or a 6-degree spot, and it works in manual as well as in shutter priority.

The meter is uncoupled: it shows an exposure value in the finder and you set the rings yourself. It focuses by coupled rangefinder to 0.85m and weighs 598g. The meter was designed around a 1.35V PX625 mercury cell and now needs a substitute.

name: Olympus AF-1
summary: A weatherproof autofocus compact Olympus released in 1986, sold in the US as the Infinity.
description: The lens is a Zuiko 35mm f/2.8, four elements in four groups, focused from 0.75m by active infrared with a focus lock. A clamshell cover powers it, in the manner of the XA.

Exposure is programmed from EV8 to EV17 at ISO 100, and film speed comes off the DX code from ISO 50 to 3200. The flash fires automatically in low light and in backlight and cannot be switched off, which is the camera's one real constraint.
Olympus sold it as its first weatherproof fully automatic compact, and it picked up the nickname Nurepika, wet flash, in Japan. It runs on a CR-P2 lithium cell at about 225g.

name: Olympus Mju Zoom 105
summary: A weather-resistant zoom compact Olympus released in 1995, sold as the Stylus Zoom 105.
description: The lens is a 38 to 105mm zoom, six elements in five groups with one aspherical, opening at f/4.5 wide and f/8.9 at the long end, focusing to 0.6m by active autofocus with a focus lock.

The shutter is programmed from 4 seconds to 1/500, and there is a spot metering mode alongside auto, red-eye, fill-in and night flash. Flash reach is about 4.7m wide and 2.4m at 105mm on ISO 100 film.
Weatherproof here means splash resistant, and Olympus quotes no depth rating. On one CR123A it is about 240g at 120 by 64 by 44mm, which is small for the range and dim at the long end.

name: Olympus Mju-I
summary: The first model of Olympus's mju and Stylus compact line, with a 35mm f/3.5 lens behind a clamshell cover.
description: Maitani Yoshihisa designed it out of his own XA, and it shows: a curved shell with the lens cover built into it, small enough to close one-handed and to carry without noticing.
Everything that followed in the mju and Stylus range is a variation on this body.

name: Olympus Trip Panorama 2
summary: A cheap fixed-focus Olympus compact with a panorama mode that can be switched mid-roll.
description: The switch drops a mask in front of the film. The frame underneath is the ordinary one, so a panoramic shot is a full frame with the top and bottom thrown away.
That is worth knowing before paying anything for the name. Nothing here is wider than any other 35mm camera; it is cropped in the camera instead of afterwards.

name: Pentax Espio 120
summary: A zoom compact Pentax released around 1994, sold as the IQZoom 120.
description: The lens is a 38 to 120mm f/4 to f/8.8 zoom, nine elements in seven groups, focusing to 0.65m at the wide end and 0.85m at 120mm, with a Super Macro mode down to 0.45m.
The shutter runs 1/5 to 1/400, with a Bulb mode from half a second to ten minutes and a ten second self-timer. Loading, advance and rewind are automatic, and there is a panorama mask.
Pentax replaced it with the 120Mi in 1998.

name: Pentax Espio 120Mi
summary: A Pentax autofocus compact with a 38 to 120mm zoom, also sold as the IQZoom 120Mi.
description: It replaced the Espio 120 of 1994 and was itself replaced by the 120SW in 2001, so it sits in the middle of a line Pentax revised roughly every three years.
Its panorama mode is a mask over the ordinary frame rather than a wider one, as it is on every compact of the period that offers it.

name: Yes!Star Jam Camera
summary: A reusable point-and-shoot in translucent plastic, sold by the Chinese brand Yes!Star.
description: It works like a disposable you can reload: one fixed 31mm f/11 lens, one shutter speed of about 1/100, and a flash running off a single AA cell. Winding on and rewinding are done by hand.
It ships with a roll of Yes!Star 400, and the body comes in colors including blue and pink.
